title: BOOK THREE / CHAPTER ONE. On man, as he can be subjected to God and beatified, in common
english: BOOK THREE. On the subject, namely man, insofar as he is a citizen of the kingdom of God, capable of the right and life of God and of eternal salvation.
CHAPTER ONE. On man, as he can be subjected to God and beatified, in common.

Thus far there has been the first thing treated by the common part of sacred Theology, namely the absolutely highest and last end of man: there follows the second, namely the subject, which is man, insofar as he can, as a citizen, be subjected to God his eternal King, by whom he was created and redeemed, be united to Him, be beatified forever, and attain his highest end.

title: Ratio of order; theology directs fallen man; know thyself and know God
english: The reason of order requires that, after we have explained how great and of what kind that highest good is which is both man's most absolute happiness and his perfection, we treat here of man, the citizen of God's kingdom, because he himself is the one to whom by this discipline, built and founded upon the divinely revealed Word, we show the way by which he may decline the extreme misery into which he fell when the bond of conjunction with God was broken, and may return to the highest beatitude, righteousness, and life of God.

For since sacred Theology, dealing with the divine kingdom, does not inform both God the King and man the subject at once — as politics, dealing with a human commonwealth, informs both the prince and the subject citizen — but directs only man fallen into misery toward recovering beatitude; therefore we call its subject especially man, insofar as he is to be subjected to God his King, united to Him, and forever kept, as was declared in Book I, chapters 1 and 4-7. For in this the kingdom of God chiefly consists (Luke 17:21; Matthew 13:23; Luke 8:11; Romans 14:17-18).

We will therefore not teach everything about man that can be known of him, but only those things which declare his character in any way in order toward the kingdom of God and eternal life. And so this part of Theology will hand on that divine saying Know thyself, and thence the other no less necessary: Know GOD, your Creator and Redeemer.

title: II. Man's origin and states; summary of the kingdom's mysteries — Cap. 1 close
english: II. But here his origin and states are to be considered, through which he is led to the state of highest perfection.

For neither can the theologian attain his end unless he knows these things, and has so far explored the nature and condition of man — whose return with God his King into grace and eternal salvation he seeks — that he may know how man depends on his Creator and King; to what end and into what state he was placed and created by Him on the sixth day; how, eating the fruit of the forbidden tree which is called the knowledge of good and evil, he soon fell with his whole race; and that Christ obediently handed Himself over to death to God the Father for lost man, and on the tree of the cross became for the whole human race dead in Adam the bread of life, which by faith one may break, eat, and therewith be satisfied and beatified.

For this is the sum of all the mysteries of the kingdom of God and of Christian doctrine, which if each person, according to the measure of his faith, understood more deeply, weighed more loftily, and recalled to his mind with simple study, truly Christ with the riches of His heavenly blessings would be sought by us hungering with unsatisfiable desire, and He Himself would satisfy our hunger and thirst with His banquet.
